edges.effect_quant: Routine vitamin K prophylaxis at birth is associated with a large reduction in vitamin K deficiency bleeding risk, with older trials showing less early bleeding or coagulopathy and surveillance studies showing that VKDB becomes uncommon when prophylaxis is used.
edges.population: newborn infants receiving intramuscular vitamin K at birth
edges.mechanism: Newborn hepatic vitamin K stores are low, and intramuscular vitamin K rapidly restores the vitamin K-dependent coagulation pathway, directly lowering the chance of classic or late hemorrhagic disease.
edges.summary: Vitamin K injection at birth is one of the clearest preventive neonatal interventions in routine care. Both classic coagulation outcomes and population surveillance of vitamin K deficiency bleeding strongly support a protective effect, making this a high-confidence beneficial edge.
edges.caveats: The strongest direct randomized data are older and often focus on classic bleeding or biochemical markers rather than modern surveillance definitions of late VKDB. Even so, the direction and clinical importance of benefit are not seriously in doubt.

evidence.notes: Comparative study of oral versus injectable vitamin K in neonates.
